`starsim_data` provides national demographic data, age-structured contact matrices, and subnational administrative geography, in forms intended to be read directly into a disease model. This page introduces the main functions in the order a new user is likely to need them. None of the examples require network access.

## Installation

::: {.panel-tabset}

## pip

```bash
pip install starsim_data
```

## with spatial support

```bash
pip install "starsim_data[spatial]"
```

## from a clone

```bash
git clone https://github.com/starsimhub/starsim_data
pip install -e starsim_data
```

:::

The base installation includes approximately 14 MB of data inside the wheel. The `[spatial]` extra additionally installs `geopandas`, `pyogrio` and `rastertoolkit`, which are needed only for the full geometry and population rasters described in [Spatial data](user-guide/spatial.qmd).

## Listing what is available

```{python}
import starsim_data as ssd

ssd.list_datasets(detailed=True)[['dataset', 'description', 'access', 'locations']]
```

The `access` column says how you get each dataset. **Bundled** data is inside the package and reads instantly, with no network access. **Fetched** data is prepared by this package but kept out of it to save space; it is downloaded from the package's own releases the first time it is used. **Downloaded** data comes from its original publisher, such as the UN, and is also cached after the first use. [Bundled, fetched and downloaded data](user-guide/access.qmd) explains the difference.

## Loading a dataset

```{python}
deaths = ssd.load('kenya', which='deaths')
deaths.head()
```

The result is a `sciris.dataframe`, which subclasses `pandas.DataFrame`, so ordinary pandas operations apply. The column names follow the UN's own conventions rather than any introduced by this package: `Time`, `Sex`, `AgeGrpStart` and `mx` are the names used in World Population Prospects, and they are also the names Starsim's demographic modules expect.

Contact matrices are returned as square frames whose rows and columns are indexed by the start age of each bin:

```{python}
matrix = ssd.load('kenya', which='prem2021')
matrix.iloc[:5, :5]
```

This allows selection by age rather than by position:

```{python}
matrix.loc[25, 30]   # daily contacts between the 25-29 and 30-34 bins
```

## Specifying locations

The canonical name is not required. ISO codes, official names, common abbreviations, and French, Spanish or Portuguese names are all recognized, and accents, case and punctuation are ignored.

```{python}
[ssd.resolve(name) for name in
 ['USA', 'US', 'united states', 'United States of America', 'Etats-Unis']]
```

```{python}
[ssd.resolve(name) for name in ["Côte d'Ivoire", 'cote divoire', 'Ivory Coast', 'CIV']]
```

A name that does not match raises an error rather than resolving to the nearest candidate, though the error does suggest possibilities: `ssd.load('Keyna', which='deaths')` gives "location 'Keyna' not found (did you mean: Kenya, China, Ghana?)".

The reasoning behind this division of labour — an exact table performs the resolution, and approximate matching only contributes to the error message — is discussed in [Locations](user-guide/locations.qmd).

## Inspecting the data visually

Plotting the data before using it is a straightforward way to detect a mistaken country or a units error.

```{python}
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 8
#| out-width: 100%
ssd.plot('kenya');
```

The summary figure shows the age pyramid, the crude birth rate over time, the mortality curve by sex, and the contact matrix. Individual panels can be drawn on their own using `which=`.

```{python}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5
#| out-width: 100%
ssd.plot('kenya', which='deaths', year=2050);
```

## Attribution

Each dataset records its own source, license and citation, stored alongside the data rather than kept separately:

```{python}
prov = ssd.provenance('prem2021')
{k: prov[k] for k in ['source', 'license', 'citation']}
```

The same information is attached to every frame returned by `load()`:

```{python}
deaths.attrs['provenance'].license
```

[Provenance and reproducibility](user-guide/provenance.qmd) describes this in more detail.

## Subnational geography

Administrative geography is also bundled, in the form of a node table giving the position and extent of each administrative unit:

```{python}
nodes = ssd.load_nodes('kenya', level=1)
nodes.head()
```

```{python}
ssd.distances('kenya', level=1).iloc[:4, :4].round(1)
```

Centroids, areas and a distance matrix are available without any geospatial dependency and without downloading anything. Polygon geometry is a separate, optional step, described in [Spatial data](user-guide/spatial.qmd).

## Data that is not bundled

The bundled demographic series consist of decadal snapshots of the Medium variant. Annual resolution, complete life tables, and other projection variants are available through `download()`, which downloads and caches the UN's bulk files:

```python
ssd.download('kenya', which='deaths', years=(2000, 2025))  # annual rather than decadal
ssd.download('kenya', which='life_table', years=2020)      # qx, lx, ex, and the rest
ssd.download('kenya', which='births', variant='High')      # a different projection variant
```

The page [Bundled, fetched and downloaded data](user-guide/access.qmd) covers the distinction, and we encourage you to read that next.
